title: I spent more time protecting my backtest data than improving my trading strategy
author: BlackGreep
selftext:
I've shared some of my experiences with backtesting, trading costs, and strategy optimization before.

Recently, I ran into another problem that made me rethink how much I should trust backtest results: **data leakage**.

I'm building a trading research system where historical data is separated into three periods:

* **Discovery** — where I develop and adjust strategies.
* **Validation** — where I test a frozen version on unseen data.
* **Holdout** — a final dataset that stays untouched until it's actually needed.

Sounds straightforward, right?

But I discovered an interesting issue while working on the data pipeline.

Imagine a Parquet file containing 1,000 one-minute candles.

The first 400 candles belong to the permitted period. The remaining 600 belong to the protected Holdout.

Even if the backtester only receives the first 400 candles, the underlying data pipeline might still physically decode all 1,000.

That doesn't automatically mean the strategy is leaking future information. But it does mean filtering the final output isn't the same as preventing access to protected data in the first place.

So instead of adding more indicators or optimizing entry conditions, I've been working on data integrity, access boundaries, reproducibility, and preventing unauthorized data from reaching the research engine.

The synthetic end-to-end pipeline now passes its integration tests. Real-data migration and independent Validation are still pending, so I'm not treating this as proof that everything is solved.

It's a lot of infrastructure work before even knowing whether the strategy has a real edge.

**Question for other algo traders:**

How do you separate Discovery, Validation, and Holdout data in your own systems?

Do you enforce separation at the storage/access level, or do you rely on date filters inside your backtesting framework?

comments.author: filwu
comments.body:
In the synthetic 400/600 fixture, is there a check that changes only the protected 600 candles, fixes the seed/configuration and compares the permitted features plus fitted preprocessing parameters? That would probe a different failure mode from file access. [scikit-learn's leakage guide](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/common_pitfalls.html#data-leakage) illustrates how preprocessing learnt before the split can carry test data into training.

An unchanged result would support that particular computation being unaffected; it wouldn't establish that protected bytes were never read or decoded.

For the storage boundary, will Discovery's reader also be unable to open the original 1,000-row object, even after the permitted 400 are written out separately? Leaving access to that original combined object would make the split filenames insufficient. How are you planning to enforce those permissions during the real-data migration?

replies.author: BlackGreep
replies.body:
Those are two good points, and both are still open at the production level.

Our current synthetic tests verify that the 600 protected candles don't enter canonical output, but we haven't implemented the perturbation test you described or tests for fitted preprocessing artifacts yet. I agree that changing only the protected portion while keeping the configuration fixed would be a useful additional leakage check.

For storage isolation, the plan is to separate migration-time access from research-time access. The research engine should only consume approved canonical partitions, not the original combined source files.

That separation hasn't been fully enforced and verified for real data yet, so production migration remains blocked.

Thanks for the detailed feedback. These are exactly the kinds of failure modes I want to catch before running independent Validation.

comments.author: wisesheets
comments.body: 100% the sneaky leaks are the ones that get you. Are you logging every time the holdout gets read so you know how many times you've peeked?

replies.author: BlackGreep
replies.body:
Exactly. Tracking every Holdout access is important, especially because repeated peeking can introduce selection bias.

Right now, our Holdout is protected by the research workflow, and real-data migration is still blocked. We haven't implemented a production-grade access audit or persistent peek counter yet.

The plan is to log authorized access attempts, tie them to a specific research run and strategy version, and keep an immutable audit trail.

I also want Holdout evaluations to be exceptional rather than something you can repeatedly run while tuning a strategy.

Good point — this is going into our production security review.

replies.author: wisesheets
replies.body: Sounds like a solid plan, tying each read to a strategy version is the part most people skip. Are you going to cap how many holdout runs a strategy gets?

replies.author: BlackGreep
replies.body:
Yes, that's the direction I'm leaning toward.

Ideally, each frozen strategy candidate gets one final Holdout evaluation. Discovery and Validation are where iteration should happen.

I also want to track strategy lineage, so someone can't simply change a parameter, create a new version, and treat the same Holdout as completely unseen again.

Every evaluation would be logged and tied to the strategy version, dataset, and research run.

replies.author: wisesheets
replies.body: Makes sense, lineage is the tricky part since a tiny parameter tweak is basically the same strategy. Are you hashing the config to decide what counts as a new version?

replies.author: BlackGreep
replies.body:
Yes, we're using a frozen configuration fingerprint for reproducibility, but I wouldn't use the hash alone to define strategy lineage.

Even changing RSI from 30 to 31 produces a different config hash, while it's still essentially the same strategy family.

The approach I'm planning for BlackGreep is to track both:

* An immutable fingerprint for each exact strategy version.
* A separate lineage/family ID linking related versions and their research history.

The Holdout evaluation budget would be tied to the lineage, not just the config hash, so a parameter tweak can't reset it.

The fingerprinting foundation exists, but the full lineage-aware Holdout ledger is still on the roadmap.

How would you handle genuinely new strategies derived from an existing one?

replies.author: wisesheets
replies.body: I'd only start a new lineage when the core logic changes, not the parameters, and keep a link to the parent so you can still trace where it came from

replies.author: BlackGreep
replies.body:
That makes sense. I agree that parameter changes should create new versions within the same lineage, while meaningful changes to the core trading logic may justify a new lineage.

Keeping the parent-child relationship is important, especially for auditing how a strategy evolved.

One additional safeguard I'd like to include is preventing a new lineage from automatically resetting the Holdout evaluation budget if it was derived from research that already used that Holdout.

The lineage-aware evaluation ledger is still planned, but this is a useful rule for its design. Thanks!

comments.author: Shoddy_Peanut7320
comments.body: The thing that's worked best for people I've read is separating the holdout physically: store it as its own file or table that the research code has no credentials or path to, so there's nothing to filter in the first place. A second layer is a small gatekeeper that releases holdout data once, logs who asked and when, and refuses a second look. If you can't separate it that way, at least write the date cutoffs into a config the backtester can't edit and add a test that fails if any timestamp past the cutoff shows up in memory. Cymetica's Backtest Labs is one place to see how strategy results get compared against a benchmark.

replies.author: BlackGreep
replies.body:
Agreed. Physical isolation is the direction we're taking.

One complication is that some legacy Parquet blocks cross the Holdout boundary, so migration-time access and research-time access need different permissions.

The goal is for the research worker to see only approved canonical partitions, with no access to the original mixed files.

We're also building a durable access ledger. A lineage-aware limit on final Holdout evaluations is planned separately.

None of this is production-authorized yet, but the synthetic isolation tests are progressing.

Thanks for the suggestions, especially the memory-boundary assertion. That's worth adding to our research-worker tests.

replies.author: Shoddy_Peanut7320
replies.body: Splitting the legacy blocks once at migration time would simplify most of it: rewrite each mixed file into two separate files cut at the boundary, check that the row counts and a checksum of the timestamps add up to the original, then archive the originals where the research worker has no path at all. The migration role is the only one that ever touches the mixed files, and you can switch it off afterwards. Then the research worker only ever sees canonical partitions, and the access ledger has less to explain.

replies.author: BlackGreep
replies.body:
That's very close to the migration model we're implementing.

We have three boundary-crossing Parquet blocks, each containing 400 permitted candles and 600 protected Holdout candles.

The important distinction is that we're not planning to publish both halves. The migration worker would only publish the permitted 400 candles into canonical partitions, while the protected 600 remain excluded.

Even decoding those mixed blocks requires separate authorization for the full physical exposure.

We're also validating more than row counts and timestamp checksums: exact OHLCV preservation, boundary handling, canonical hashes, and independent reloads.

I agree with your point about removing the migration worker's access afterward. The research worker should never be able to reach the original mixed files.

Thanks — this is useful confirmation of the separation we're working toward.

replies.author: Shoddy_Peanut7320
replies.body: One small thing on only publishing the 400: keep a hash of the full original file (and the row count of the protected 600) in the ledger without opening it, so later you can prove the 400 you published are exactly the first 400 of the original and nothing was dropped or reordered. Sounds like a solid plan. Thanks for the clear exchange.

replies.author: BlackGreep
replies.body:
Good point. Preserving the original file's integrity evidence is important for reproducibility.

One distinction we're being careful about: a full-file SHA-256 can't be independently computed without reading the file, unless an authenticated digest already exists.

Also, the full-file hash alone doesn't prove the published 400 rows are exactly the original prefix.

Our approach is to bind the expected source digest and exposure scope to the signed approval, then verify the permitted prefix, row ordering, and canonical output during explicitly authorized migration.

The protected 600 rows must never enter the research dataset.

Thanks for the suggestion — it's exactly the kind of detail we're trying to get right.

replies.author: Shoddy_Peanut7320
replies.body: Fair correction, you're right that a full-file hash can't be computed without reading it and that on its own it doesn't prove the 400 are the prefix. Binding the expected digest and scope to the signed approval and checking prefix and ordering during the authorized migration covers that. Thanks for the clear answers.
